prompt: What does `typeof null` return, and what is `null`?
hint: The section calls the answer a mistake.

choices.text: `"null"`, and it is its own primitive type
choices.why: The type is its own, but `typeof` does not say so.
Right. A bug from 1995 that pages now depend on.
`typeof undefined` is `"undefined"`; `null` answers differently.
`null` is not an object; the answer is a historical mistake.

prompt: How do you tell an array from a plain object?
hint: `typeof` gives the same answer for both.

choices.why: `typeof` never returns `"array"`; arrays are `"object"`.
Both arrays and plain objects are instances of `Object`.
Right: it printed `true false` for `[]` and `{}`.
An empty array has length 0, and an object could have a `length` property.

prompt: Match each situation to the value JavaScript or the programmer gives.
hint: One of them is written on purpose.

pairs.left: A declared `let` name with nothing assigned
A book that deliberately has no cover yet

prompt: `const title = "Iracema"; title.toUpperCase();` What is `title` afterwards?
hint: Can an operation change a primitive in place?

choices.why: Right. The method returned a new string that nobody kept.

choices.text: `"IRACEMA"`, because the method changes the string
choices.why: No operation changes a primitive; it returns a new one.
Nothing was reassigned, so `const` has nothing to refuse.

choices.text: `undefined`, since the result was not stored
choices.why: The name still holds its original string.

hint: What format are numbers stored in?

choices.text: `===` compares the types, and the result is a string
choices.why: The result is a number.

choices.text: JavaScript rounds every addition to two places
choices.why: It rounds nothing; `toFixed` is how you ask for that.

choices.text: Binary floating point cannot store one tenth exactly
choices.why: Right. The sum lands a hair away from the stored 0.3.

choices.text: A bug in Node that browsers do not have

prompt: `cents.js` multiplied a price of 1990 cents by 3. What total, in cents, did it print?
An API sends a database id of `9007199254740993` as a number. What does JavaScript hold after reading it?

choices.text: Exactly that id, since it has no fractional part
choices.why: Whole numbers are only exact up to `9007199254740991`.

choices.text: `Infinity`, because it is too large to store
choices.why: It is far below the largest number the format holds; it loses precision, not range.

choices.text: A nearby number, off by one
choices.why: Right. Past the safe limit, `2 ** 53 + 1` came back as `2 ** 53`.

choices.text: A BigInt, which JavaScript switches to for large numbers
choices.why: BigInts are written with an `n` on purpose; nothing switches automatically.

prompt: What does `-7 % 3` give?
hint: The remainder keeps one side's sign.

choices.why: That is the mathematical modulo; `%` keeps the left side's sign.
Right: the sign of `-7`.
That is `7 % 3`.
The remainder of a negative number is defined.

prompt: Which conversion of the text `"42px"` gives `42`?
hint: One of them reads from the left and stops.

choices.why: It converts the whole value or gives `NaN`, which it did.
Right: it stops at the `p`.
That turns it into a string, which it already was.
That gives `true`, as every non-empty string does.

prompt: A form field is left empty, and the code runs `Number(field.value)`. What comes out?
hint: The section calls it the trap.

choices.text: `NaN`, so the code can notice the field was empty
choices.why: That is what `parseFloat("")` gives; `Number` differs here.
An empty field's value is the empty string, and `Number("")` is a number.
Right. An empty field becomes zero, which is why the section checks for empty text first.
`Number` never throws on a string.

prompt: A Brazilian user types `1,5` into a price field. What does `Number("1,5")` return?

choices.text: `1.5`, since JavaScript follows the system's language
choices.why: Conversion ignores the locale; the point is the separator.

choices.text: `1`, because conversion stops at the comma
choices.why: That is `parseInt`'s and `parseFloat`'s behaviour.
The comma is not ignored; it makes the text not a number.
Right. Replace the comma with a point before converting.

prompt: To write a number for a Brazilian reader, with a comma for decimals, call `n.___("pt-BR")`.
What is `"5" + 3`, and what is `"5" - 3`?

choices.why: `+` with a string joins rather than adds.
Right. `+` joins when either side is a string; `-` only does arithmetic.
`-` converts `"5"` to the number 5, which works.
Coercion converts silently; nothing throws.

prompt: The page read `10` from a field and printed `105` for `copies + 5`. What is the right fix?

choices.text: Write `copies - -5` so the operator converts it
choices.why: It works, and it hides the conversion the section wants you to make visible.

choices.text: `Number(copies) + 5`, or convert once when reading the field
choices.why: Right: explicit, and at the point where the text enters.

choices.text: Change the input's `value` attribute to the number 10
choices.why: A field's value is always a string, whatever you write in the HTML.

choices.text: Use a template string instead of `+`
choices.why: A template joins too; it does not add.

prompt: Why is `"3" > "12"` true?
hint: Two strings, no number in sight.

choices.text: `>` converts both to numbers and 3 is greater
choices.why: 3 is less than 12; the strings were not converted.

choices.text: Strings are compared by length, and `"12"` is longer
choices.why: A longer string would then be greater, which it is not here.

choices.text: Two strings compare character by character, and `"3"` comes after `"1"`
choices.why: Right: dictionary order. `3 > "12"` converts and is false.

choices.text: It is a known bug in `>` with strings
choices.why: It is the defined rule for comparing two strings.

prompt: `0 == ""` and `0 == "0"` are both true. What is `"" == "0"`?

choices.why: That reasoning needs equality to be transitive, and `==` is not.

prompt: `const n = Number("forty");` Which test is true?

choices.why: Nothing is equal to `NaN`, itself included.
Loose equality does not change that.
`Number` returns `NaN`, which is a number.
Right. It printed `true`.

prompt: `{ title: "Iracema" } === { title: "Iracema" }` is false. What would make a comparison of two books by contents true?

choices.why: `==` also compares objects by identity; it printed `false` too.

choices.text: Comparing the properties that matter, such as `a.title === b.title`
